title: recite
text: recite takes a passage as the lines a reader sees and returns one audio file with timings for every line and word. This page builds it up in steps.

title: recite
text:
Pieces
Vāgdhenu renders text in pieces, and expects the two pādas (quarter-verses) of a half-verse as one piece, even when the book prints them on two lines. pieces(lines) groups the display lines accordingly: a piece ends after a word that contains a daṇḍa. In prose (prose=True) a piece also ends before it would pass max_syll (24) akṣaras, and in verse before a line that would take it past max_verse (44). Each piece is a list of (line_index, word) pairs, so word timings can be mapped back to their lines. A word that cleans to nothing, such as a daṇḍa or a verse number, stays in its piece and gets no time of its own. piece_text gives the cleaned text of a piece for rendering.

pieces
def pieces(
    lines, prose:bool=False, max_syll:int=24, max_verse:int=44
):
Group display lines into render pieces, each a list of (line_index, word).

word_text
def word_text(
    w

ls = ['नित्यानन्दकरी वराभयकरी सौन्दर्यरत्नाकरी', 'निर्धूताखिलघोरपावनकरी प्रत्यक्षमाहेश्वरी ।', 'प्रालेयाचलवंशपावनकरी काशीपुराधीश्वरी', 'भिक्षां देहि कृपावलम्बनकरी मातान्नपूर्णेश्वरी ॥ १ ॥']
ps = pieces(ls)
test_eq(len(ps), 2)
test_eq({i for i,_ in ps[0]}, {0, 1})
test_eq(ps[1][-1], (3, '॥'))
test_eq(len(pieces(['उपदेशं व्याख्यास्यामः॥'], prose=True)), 1)
assert all(sum(n_syll(word_text(w)) for _,w in p) <= 24 for p in pieces(['क '*60], prose=True))

title: recite
text:
Lines from words
Word timings come back per piece. line_times(n, ps, words) turns them into one dict(s, e, w) per display line: the start of its first timed word, the end of its last, and the list of its words with their times. A line with no words gets None.


source

line_times
def line_times(
    n, ps, words
):
One dict(s, e, w) per line from the pieces’ word timings, or None for a line with no words.



ps = [[(0,'क'), (0,'ख'), (1,'ग')], [(1,'॥')]]
lt = line_times(3, ps, [[['क',0,100], ['ख',100,200], ['ग',300,400]], [['॥',400,400]]])
test_eq([lt[0]['s'], lt[0]['e'], lt[1]['s'], lt[1]['e']], [0, 200, 300, 400])
test_eq(lt[2], None)

title: recite
text:
Reciting sections
A section is a passage, such as a verse with its commentary, that becomes one stretch of audio. recite_section splits it into parts, each recited in a single voice, either chanted or read. By default the section is split into verses with verses, each ending on a line with a double daṇḍa, and each verse is scanned by ganapati to find its metre. ganapati applies the rules of the śloka, where Vāgdhenu’s own detector accepted a 32-syllable prose sentence as anuṣṭubh, and it recognises the āryā family, whose metres count syllable lengths instead of syllables.
part_voice then picks the voice. A metre with a reference in Vāgdhenu’s bank is chanted against that reference, another syllable-counted metre (a vṛtta) is chanted against vasantatilakā, and an āryā-family metre, or no metre at all, is read against the anuṣṭubh reference. You can give the parts yourself as parts=[dict(lines=[...], meter=...)], with line indices, and kind='chant' or kind='read' makes the whole section one voice. recite_part renders one part, keeping the best of tries seeds by Su-śrotā’s character error rate, and returns the timings of its lines. shift moves a set of timings later, so that each part’s timings count from the start of the whole recording.

shift
def shift(
    info, off
):
Move all the timings in info off milliseconds later.


The cell below checks this bookkeeping with a stand-in chanter and ear, without the models. A verse that scans is chanted, the prose line after it is read, and the second part’s timings start after the first part plus the gap. Parts given explicitly get the voice their metre calls for.
recite(ch, ear, sections) is the top-level call. Each section is a dict with lines and optionally kind, ref and parts. It recites every section, joins them with gap (1.2) seconds of silence, and returns the Recitation and a list with one dict per section: its kind (chant, read or mixed), its first part’s ref, its worst cer, its parts, and its lines timings.

from vachaka.core import Recitation
from vachaka.check import Ear
class FakeCh:
    gap, prose_gap = 0.5, 0.3
    def meter(self, lines): return 'anushtubh' if len(lines) == 2 else ''
    def bank_ref(self, name): return {'anuṣṭubh': 'anuṣṭubh', 'mālinī': 'mālinī'}.get(name)
    def render(self, ps, ref, seed, gap): return Recitation(np.zeros(len(ps)*24000, np.float32), [(i*1000, i*1000+900) for i in range(len(ps))], ps)
class FakeEar:
    def hear(self, audio, sr): return ''
    heard = Ear.heard   # best_of hears a render a piece at a time
    def words(self, rec, ws): return [[[w, s, e] for w in p] for (s,e),p in zip(rec.spans, ws)]
r, info = recite_section(FakeCh(), FakeEar(), ['धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः ।', 'मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय ॥ १ ॥', 'इति प्रश्नः ॥'])
test_eq([p['kind'] for p in info['parts']], ['chant', 'read'])
test_eq(info['kind'], 'mixed')
test_eq(info['lines'][2]['s'], 2000 + 800)           # two 1 s pieces, then the gap
_, info = recite_section(FakeCh(), FakeEar(), ['क ख ग', 'घ ङ च ॥', 'छ ज झ ।'])
test_eq([p['kind'] for p in info['parts']], ['chant', 'read'])  # the line after the verse is its own part, and scans as nothing
ps = [dict(lines=[0, 1], meter='mālinī'), dict(lines=[2], meter='āryā'), dict(lines=[3], meter='śikhariṇī'), dict(lines=[4], meter=None)]
_, info = recite_section(FakeCh(), FakeEar(), ['क ।', 'ख ॥', 'ग ॥', 'घ ॥', 'ङ ।'], parts=ps)
test_eq([(p['kind'], p['ref']) for p in info['parts']], [('chant', 'mālinī'), ('read', 'anuṣṭubh'), ('chant', 'vasantatilaka'), ('read', 'anuṣṭubh')])

Recite sections, each dict(lines=..., kind=..., ref=...), as one Recitation with timings per section.

title: recite
text:
CLI
vachaka-recite jobs.jsonl results.jsonl renders a file of jobs, one JSON object per line. Each job is dict(id, out, sections), where sections is what recite takes. It writes the audio to out (mp3 or wav) and appends dict(id, out, ms, sections) to the results file, with sections holding the timings. A job whose id is already in the results is skipped, so a stopped run carries on where it left off.
The options are --voice (steer), --tries (3) and --max_cer (0.08) for re-rendering, --pace (1.15), --pitch (1.0, so one semitone up by default) and --fx, the sound treatment from core.FX (warm, or none for the raw render).


source

recite_cli
def recite_cli(
    jobs:str, results:str, voice:str='steer', tries:int=3, max_cer:float=0.08, fx:str='warm', pace:float=1.15,
    pitch:float=1.0

Render each job in the JSON lines file jobs and append its timings to results.

title: check
text:
A text-to-speech model sometimes mumbles, skips a word or garbles a line, and nobody can listen to thousands of renders. This module uses a speech recogniser to check them instead: it transcribes each render, measures how far the transcript is from the text, re-renders the bad ones, and finds where each word sits in the audio.
The recogniser is Su-śrotā, IndicConformer fine-tuned on śāstric Sanskrit. Its CTC output layer covers all 22 IndicConformer languages, and Sanskrit is the 256 columns starting at 4096, with the blank token at 5632. The checkpoint is configured for AI4Bharat’s fork of NeMo (a multilingual tokenizer and a multisoftmax decoder), so Ear rewrites the configuration for the standard NeMo: the tokenizer type becomes agg, the settings only the fork understands are removed, and the weights are loaded without requiring every key to match. Only the encoder and the CTC output layer are used. Install it with pip install 'vachaka[check]'.

title: check
text:
Comparing text
Su-śrotā does not write exactly what the text says. It leaves out daṇḍas, digits and the avagraha (ऽ), and writes a word-final म् as an anusvāra (ं). norm(s) brings any text to that form, so a transcript can be compared with its source fairly. cer(ref, hyp) is the character error rate: the edit distance (lev, the number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions) between the two normalised texts, divided by the length of the reference. Spaces are ignored, because Sanskrit texts differ in where they split words joined by sandhi.


source

norm
def norm(
    s
):
Text in the form Su-śrotā writes it: NFC, without accents, digits, daṇḍas or avagraha, and with word-final म् as anusvāra.



test_eq(norm('चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः ॥ २ ॥'), 'चोदनालक्षणो र्थो धर्मः')
test_eq(norm('कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्'), 'कंसचाणूरमर्दनं')



source

cer
def cer(
    ref, hyp
):
The character error rate of hyp against ref, both normalised and with spaces ignored.




source

lev
def lev(
    a, b
):
Edit distance between sequences a and b.



test_eq(lev('kitten', 'sitting'), 3)
test_eq(cer('अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा', 'अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा'), 0)
assert 0 < cer('तस्य निमित्तपरीष्टिः', 'तस्य निमित्तपरेष्टिः') < 0.1

Ear
Ear() loads Su-śrotā on the CPU. hear(audio, sr) transcribes audio and returns the normalised text. post(audio, sr) returns the model’s raw output for each 40 ms frame, the log-probability of the blank and of each of the 256 Sanskrit tokens, together with the frame length in milliseconds; words below uses it to align.

Su-śrotā on the CPU, for transcripts and word timings.

title: check
text:
Best of a few seeds
Each render uses a random seed, and a different seed gives a slightly different performance. best_of(render, ear, text) calls render(seed=...) up to tries (3) times with different seeds, measures each result’s character error rate against text, and keeps the best, stopping early once one is at or below max_cer (0.08). The rate is stored on the result as Recitation.cer.
ear.heard(rec) transcribes a render one piece at a time, using its spans, and joins the results. Transcribing the whole render at once fails on long runs of nearly identical lines, such as a tarpaṇa or the eight directions of a digvandana: the recogniser loses its place, and good renders scored between 0.47 and 0.76.


source

Ear.heard
def heard(
    rec
):
Transcribe rec one piece of its spans at a time and join the transcripts.



class _E(Ear):
    def __init__(self): self.got = []
    def hear(self, audio, sr): self.got.append(len(audio)); return 'क'
e, r = _E(), AttrDict(audio=np.zeros(16000*3, np.float32), sr=16000, spans=[(0, 1000), (1500, 3000)])
test_eq(e.heard(r), 'क क'); test_eq(e.got, [16000, 24000])
test_eq(_E().heard(AttrDict(audio=np.zeros(800, np.float32), sr=16000)), 'क')



source

best_of
def best_of(
    render, ear, text, tries:int=3, max_cer:float=0.08, seed:int=60
):
Call render(seed=...) up to tries times and keep the render whose transcript is closest to text.

title: check
text:
Word timings
ear.words(rec, words) finds the start and end of each word, given a render and, for each of its pieces, the list of words as displayed. It force-aligns them, matching the known word sequence against the audio with torchaudio’s CTC aligner, inside each piece’s own span, so a badly rendered line cannot drag the timings of the others. Each word is tokenised from its cleaned form. A word with no Sanskrit tokens, such as a lone daṇḍa, gets an empty span at the end of the word before it. The result has one list per piece, of [word, start_ms, end_ms].


source

Ear.words
def words(
    rec, words
):
The [word, start_ms, end_ms] of each displayed word, for each piece of rec.


These cells need the Su-śrotā checkpoint (520 MB) and the Vāgdhenu weights, so they do not run in the tests.

from vachaka.core import Chanter
ch, ear = Chanter(), Ear()
lines = ['वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 'देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम्']
r = best_of(partial(ch.chant, lines), ear, ' '.join(lines))
r.cer, ear.words(r, [l.split() for l in lines])

title: vachaka
text:
vachaka (वाचक, “reciter”) turns Sanskrit text in Devanagari into recited audio, and tells you where every line and every word falls in that audio. It is a thin layer over two models by Prathosh A. P. Vāgdhenu is a text-to-speech model that chants: given a verse and a reference recording in the verse’s metre, it sings the verse to that metre’s tune. It is a fine-tune of IndicF5 with a BigVGAN-v2 vocoder, the part that turns the model’s output into a waveform. Su-śrotā is a Sanskrit speech recogniser, IndicConformer fine-tuned on śāstric Sanskrit. Vāgdhenu does the speaking. Su-śrotā listens back: it transcribes each render and compares the transcript with the text, so a bad render can be thrown away and tried again, and it finds where each word starts and ends.
vachaka was written for VedicReader, which has thousands of Sanskrit verses and sūtras that nobody has recorded. There the input is a work’s lines as they are displayed, and the output must be one audio file plus a [start, end] time for every line and word, so the reader can highlight the text as it plays. vachaka.recite does exactly that.

title: vachaka
text:
Listen
These clips come from a trial run over VedicReader’s texts. The voice is synthetic, and it is that of Vāgdhenu’s author. CER, the character error rate, is the share of characters Su-śrotā got wrong when it transcribed the clip, compared with the text: 0.0 means every character was heard as written. The audio players work on the docs site; GitHub and PyPI show only the text. Each clip says whether it was chanted or read, and which reference recording it was rendered against.

Annapūrṇāṣṭakam, verse 2 (śārdūlavikrīḍita)

इति स्तुत्या सुसंहृष्टो मुनिस्तत्त्वविदां वरः।अथादिदेश सच्छास्त्रं सारं यज्ज्योतिषां शुभम्॥ ३॥

उपदेशं व्याख्यास्यामः॥

One sūtra, two references
Nyāyasūtra 1.1.2 rendered twice. Vāgdhenu ships two reference recordings for prose (gadya), but its author renders prose against the anuṣṭubh reference instead, having found that the gadya references drop the starts of words. When recite reads prose it follows the author and uses anuṣṭubh. Judge for yourself:

title: vachaka
text:
Numbers
Measured on an Apple M3 Max with 36 GB of memory, running Vāgdhenu’s main network (a diffusion transformer, or DiT) on the GPU through MPS and the vocoder on the CPU.







loading Vāgdhenu
10 to 17 s


rendering, warm
about 5.5 s per second of audio (a 9.5 s anuṣṭubh verse in 50 to 57 s)


share of render time in the DiT
77% (the rest is BigVGAN on the CPU)


loading Su-śrotā
9 s


transcribing a 10 s clip on the CPU
0.4 s


alignment resolution
40 ms (Su-śrotā’s frame)



At that speed an hour of recitation takes five to six hours on a laptop. A CUDA GPU is much faster, and Vāgdhenu’s author renders on one.
The trial rendered 27 sections, 293 s of audio in all, from a stotra, three jyotiṣa books, the Jaimini Sūtras and the Nyāyasūtra, keeping the best of up to three renders per section. “Exact” counts the sections Su-śrotā transcribed with no error.

Two cautions. Su-śrotā comes from the same lab as Vāgdhenu and its training data includes recordings of a TTS speaker, so it may hear Vāgdhenu more kindly than a person would. A low CER says the words are there, not that the chant sounds good. And a section whose metre is not detected (an āryā, or a verse split over three lines) is read as prose, which sounds flatter than a chant. Listen before you publish.

title: vachaka
text:
Install
pip install vachaka            # rendering
pip install 'vachaka[check]'   # Su-śrotā: transcripts, error rate, word timings
vachaka needs Python 3.10 to 3.12. The first Chanter() downloads about 1.5 GB of weights from the Hugging Face Hub, and fetches the source code of Vāgdhenu, BigVGAN and IndicF5 at fixed commits into ~/.cache/vachaka (set VACHAKA_CACHE to put it elsewhere). None of the three is on PyPI, and the package called f5-tts there is not IndicF5. Su-śrotā is another 520 MB. Writing mp3 files needs ffmpeg.

title: vachaka
text:
Use
Chanter loads Vāgdhenu. chant sings a verse given as a list of its lines, picking the tune from the verse’s metre, and read reads prose. Both return a Recitation, which holds the audio and one (start, end) span in milliseconds for each line or chunk of prose, and can be saved as wav or mp3:
from vachaka.core import Chanter
ch = Chanter()                        # cuda, then mps, then cpu
r = ch.chant(['वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 'देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम्'])
r.spans                               # [(0, 4230), (4980, 9550)]: one span per line, in ms
r.save('krishna.mp3')
ch.read('अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा । चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः ।', ref='anuṣṭubh').save('mimamsa.mp3')
Ear loads Su-śrotā. best_of renders up to three times with different random seeds and keeps the render whose transcript is closest to the text, ear.hear shows what Su-śrotā heard, and ear.words gives each word’s start and end in milliseconds:
from vachaka.check import Ear, best_of
ear = Ear()
lines = ['वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 'देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम्']
r = best_of(lambda seed: ch.chant(lines, seed=seed), ear, ' '.join(lines))
r.cer                                 # 0.0
ear.hear(r.audio, r.sr)               # 'वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनं देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुं'
ear.words(r, [l.split() for l in lines])
# [[['वसुदेवसुतं', 120, 1279], ['देवं', 1279, 1878], ['कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 1878, 3756]],
#  [['देवकीपरमानन्दं', 5100, 7018], ['कृष्णं', 7018, 7697], ['वन्दे', 7697, 8217], ['जगद्गुरुम्', 8217, 9056]]]
recite does all of this for whole sections of a text. You give it each section’s lines exactly as displayed, with daṇḍas (the । and ॥ that end half-verses and verses), verse numbers and accent marks left in. It decides for each verse whether to chant or read it, and returns the audio together with every line’s span and words:
from vachaka.recite import recite
rec, info = recite(ch, ear, [dict(lines=['नित्यानन्दकरी वराभयकरी सौन्दर्यरत्नाकरी', 'निर्धूताखिलघोरपावनकरी प्रत्यक्षमाहेश्वरी ।',
                                         'प्रालेयाचलवंशपावनकरी काशीपुराधीश्वरी', 'भिक्षां देहि कृपावलम्बनकरी मातान्नपूर्णेश्वरी ॥ १ ॥'])])
info[0]['kind'], info[0]['ref'], info[0]['lines'][0]   # 'chant', 'shardulavikridita', {'s': ..., 'e': ..., 'w': [...]}
For batches there is a command-line tool that reads and writes JSON lines and can be stopped and restarted: vachaka-recite jobs.jsonl results.jsonl, where each job is dict(id, out, sections). See recite.

title: vachaka
text:
How it works
recite first groups the display lines into pieces, the units Vāgdhenu renders. A piece ends after a word carrying a daṇḍa, so the two pādas (quarter-verses) of a half-verse printed on two lines render together, as Vāgdhenu expects. Each verse, which ends at a double daṇḍa, is scanned by ganapati to find its metre. A verse in one of the metres Vāgdhenu has a reference recording for is chanted against that recording. Any other syllable-counted metre (a vṛtta) is chanted against the vasantatilakā reference. An āryā, whose metre counts syllable lengths instead, or anything that does not scan, is read as prose in chunks of at most 24 akṣaras (syllables). So a commentary that quotes a verse chants the verse and reads the rest.
Vāgdhenu renders each piece separately and joins them with short silences, and vachaka records where each piece landed. Su-śrotā then transcribes the render one piece at a time, and if the character error rate is above 8%, the part is rendered again with another seed, keeping the best of three. Finally the words of each piece are force-aligned, matched against the audio with torchaudio’s CTC aligner over Su-śrotā’s output, inside that piece’s span, so one bad line cannot pull the rest out of place.
Two things had to be patched to run this on a Mac. BigVGAN uses a transposed convolution with more than 65,536 output channels, which MPS does not support, so the vocoder runs on the CPU. And Su-śrotā’s checkpoint is configured for AI4Bharat’s fork of NeMo, so vachaka rewrites its configuration for the standard NeMo (the tokenizer type becomes agg, and the fork’s multisoftmax settings are removed) and uses only the encoder and the CTC output layer, reading the Sanskrit columns 4096 to 4351.

title: vachaka
text:
Limits
There are no Vedic svaras (pitch accents): Vāgdhenu chants in the classical (laukika) style, and accent marks are removed before rendering. There is one voice, the model author’s; the reference recording sets the pace and melody but not the timbre. A metre outside Vāgdhenu’s set of references is chanted to vasantatilakā when ganapati recognises it as some other vṛtta, and read as prose when it is not recognised at all. Prose sounds like careful reading, not chant.

title: core
text:
This module loads Vāgdhenu and renders Sanskrit text with it. Vāgdhenu (code, weights, Apache-2.0) is a fine-tune of IndicF5, a text-to-speech model, with a BigVGAN-v2 vocoder, trained on one speaker’s chanting. Its source code, BigVGAN’s and IndicF5’s (the f5_tts package, which is not the f5-tts on PyPI) are not pip packages. So on first use fetch_src downloads each of them at a fixed commit, listed in SRCS, into the cache folder, and setup_paths puts them on sys.path. The weights come from the Hugging Face Hub. best_device picks CUDA if it is there, then Apple’s MPS, then the CPU.

title: core
text:
Text
The model reads plain Devanagari, so clean(s) removes Vedic accent marks and digits, and reduces each run of daṇḍas (। and ॥, with the verse number between them) to a single daṇḍa, keeping ॥ where there was one. Vāgdhenu has no svaras (Vedic pitch accents) and chants in the classical, laukika, style.
n_syll(s) counts the akṣaras, the syllables of Devanagari text: each independent vowel and each consonant not followed by a virāma. chunk_prose(text, max_syll) splits prose into pieces Vāgdhenu can render: first at daṇḍas, then between words, so that no piece has more than max_syll (24) akṣaras.


source

clean
def clean(
    s
):
Plain Devanagari for the model, without accents, digits or verse numbers between daṇḍas.



test_eq(clean('अग्निमी॑ळे पु॒रोहि॑तं ॥ १ ॥'), 'अग्निमीळे पुरोहितं ॥')
test_eq(clean('धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे ।'), 'धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे ।')



source

n_syll
def n_syll(
    s
):
The number of akṣaras in Devanagari s: independent vowels and consonants without a virāma.



test_eq(n_syll('कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते'), 8)



source

chunk_prose
def chunk_prose(
    text, max_syll:int=24
):
Split prose at daṇḍas, then between words, into pieces of at most max_syll akṣaras.



p = chunk_prose('अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा । चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः । तस्य निमित्तपरीष्टिः ॥')
test_eq(p, ['अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा', 'चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः', 'तस्य निमित्तपरीष्टिः'])
assert all(n_syll(c) <= 24 for c in chunk_prose('क '*80))

title: core
text:
Sound
The raw render can sound thin, so polish(src, dst, fx) applies a named sound treatment to an audio file with ffmpeg. The treatments in FX were chosen by ear for listeners, not sound engineers. Each ends by normalising loudness to -16 LUFS, so every recording plays at the same volume, and none moves any sound in time: the echo adds decay after a syllable, never delay before it, so line and word timings stay valid. warm, the default, adds a little warmth below 250 Hz, softens hissing s sounds and adds the short echo of a small room. phone brings the words forward for small speakers. plain only normalises loudness.


source

polish
def polish(
    src, dst, fx:str='warm', kbps:int=96
):
Apply the sound treatment FX[fx] to audio file src and write it to dst.



test_eq(sorted(FX), ['phone', 'plain', 'warm'])
assert all(v.endswith(LN) for v in FX.values())

title: core
text:
Recitation
A Recitation is what every render returns: the audio as a numpy array, its sample rate sr, one (start_ms, end_ms) span per piece in spans, the text of each piece in texts, and, once Su-śrotā has checked it, the character error rate cer. A piece is a line given to Chanter.chant or a chunk made by Chanter.read. ms is the length in milliseconds. save writes a wav file, or an mp3 through ffmpeg when the path ends in .mp3, optionally shifted pitch semitones and with an FX treatment; the timings stay valid. concat, or +, joins recitations with a silence between them and moves the later spans along to match.


source

Recitation
def Recitation(
    audio:numpy.ndarray, spans:list=<factory>, texts:list=<factory>, sr:int=24000, cer:float=None
)->None:
Recitation(audio: numpy.ndarray, spans: list = , texts: list = , sr: int = 24000, cer: float = None)

concat
def concat(
    recs, gap:float=0.8
):
Join recitations with gap seconds of silence between them, moving their spans to match.



a = Recitation(np.zeros(SR, np.float32), [(0, 900)], ['क'])
b = a + a
test_eq(b.ms, 2800)
test_eq(b.spans, [(0, 900), (1800, 2700)])

title: core
text:
Chanter
Chanter() loads Vāgdhenu’s network, the vocoder and the bank of reference recordings once, and then renders as often as you like. Vāgdhenu sings a text in the style of a reference recording: the reference sets the pace and melody, and the timbre is always the fine-tuned voice. The bank holds one reference for each metre Vāgdhenu supports, plus gadya references for prose.

chant(lines) sings one verse given as a list of its lines, or as a string that it splits at newlines and daṇḍas. It finds the metre with ganapati through meter, renders against that metre’s reference, and uses vasantatilakā when nothing is detected. Pass meter= to choose one. The result has one span per line.
read(text) reads prose, split by chunk_prose, against the gadya reference by default, or against another reference given as ref. The result has one span per chunk.
render(pieces, ref) is what both call: it renders already cleaned pieces against one reference.
meters() lists the metres in the bank, and bank_ref(name) finds a metre’s reference under any spelling (IAST, plain ASCII or the recording’s file name), or returns None.

pace stretches every syllable; the default of 1.15 is unhurried, for chanting along. seed picks the random seed for a render; a different seed gives a slightly different performance. voice chooses between the two fine-tuned voices in VOICES. On Apple silicon the main network runs on MPS and BigVGAN on the CPU, because MPS has no transposed convolution with more than 65,536 output channels.


source

Chanter
def Chanter(
    voice:str='steer', device:NoneType=None, nfe:int=64, speed:float=0.9, gap:float=0.55, prose_gap:float=0.3,
    tail:float=0.18, fade:float=0.12, pad:float=0.5, pace:float=1.15
):
Renders Sanskrit verse and prose to audio with Vāgdhenu, with a time span per line.


Rendering needs the weights, about 1.5 GB downloaded on first use, and takes several times real time on Apple silicon, so these cells do not run in the tests.

ch = Chanter()
r = ch.chant(['वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनम्', 'देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम्'])
r.spans, r.save('/tmp/krishna.mp3')


ch.read('अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा । चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः ।').save('/tmp/mimamsa.mp3')
